summary: At nearly ten million residents spread across more than 4,000 square miles, Los Angeles County is larger in population than 40 individual U.S. states — yet its geography is so fractured by mountain ranges, canyon systems, and coastal bluffs that daily life in one corner can feel utterly unrelated to another. The San Gabriel Mountains rise above 10,000 feet barely 30 miles from the Pacific, and the county encompasses everything from the flat, logistics-heavy basin around the ports of Long Beach and San Pedro to the narrow, winding canyon roads of the Santa Monica Mountains. That sheer scale shapes the commute reality: major employers span entertainment, aerospace, healthcare systems like Kaiser and UCLA Health, the massive port complex, and SpaceX in Hawthorne, but switching jobs often means switching freeways and adding 45 minutes each way. Housing math is stark — at a median home value of $783,300 against median household income of $87,760, the price-to-income ratio exceeds 8.9, meaning even dual-income households face a long savings runway to buy, while median rent at $1,893 consumes roughly 26% of gross monthly income. With an annual average of 10 hours of daily sunshine and daytime highs averaging 74°F, the 300-plus clear days a year are real — but so is the tradeoff that the county's motor-vehicle theft rate of 621 per 100,000 is notably elevated. Los Angeles County is essentially a constellation of small cities and unincorporated pockets stitched together by freeways, which means "moving to L.A." is less a single decision than a series of micro-decisions about which fragment of a sprawling, sun-drenched, extraordinarily expensive mosaic you can actually reach your job from.
